Few readers pause to admire the index at the back of a book, yet it is one of the most ingenious tools ever devised for navigating knowledge. Its lineage begins not with printing but with the cloisters and universities of the thirteenth century. Novices and preachers then needed to locate passages swiftly in a burgeoning mass of texts. Learned clerics responded by compiling alphabetical inventories of key terms, each accompanied by a reference to where the term occurred.
Such early indexes faced a formidable obstacle. Because every manuscript was transcribed by hand, the same passage fell on a different page in each copy, so references usually had to point to chapters or sections rather than to pages. Only when printing produced thousands of identical copies did the page number become a ____ address, and the index as we know it could flourish.
Not everyone embraced the innovation. Critics lamented that readers who leapt straight to the index would skim books rather than scrutinize them, plucking out fragments without comprehending the whole.
The grievance sounds eerily familiar today, when a search engine can retrieve a single sentence from a vast library. "Every tool that makes knowledge easier to reach," one historian of the book has observed, "invites the apprehension that it will render knowledge shallower."

Every search query, streamed film, and chatbot reply hinges on buildings most people never glimpse: data centers, cavernous warehouses crammed with servers that hum incessantly. For years their appetite for electricity grew more sluggishly than many had feared, as engineers wrung more computing out of each watt. The boom in artificial intelligence has upended that picture. Training and operating gargantuan AI models requires specialized chips that consume far more power than conventional servers, and technology companies have been scrambling to erect ever larger facilities to accommodate them.
The International Energy Agency estimated that data centers used roughly 1.5 percent of the world's electricity in 2024, and projected that their consumption could roughly double by the end of the decade. The figure sounds innocuous, but the demand is intensely localized. In some regions a single new campus can devour as much power as a mid-sized city, compelling utilities to postpone the retirement of fossil-fuel plants or even to construct new ones. In such places <u>the promise of clean computing</u> can collide with the arithmetic of the local grid.
Water is a less conspicuous concern. Servers emit intense heat, and many facilities cool them by evaporating water, consuming prodigious volumes in the process. In arid areas, residents and farmers have begun to question whether a server farm should take precedence over their own needs during a drought.
Companies retort that they are signing contracts for wind, solar and even nuclear power and piloting cooling systems that recycle water. "Such pledges are only as dependable as the grids and rivers they draw on," one energy analyst countered. Either way, the cloud turns out to be firmly tethered to the ground.

In 1977 NASA launched two small spacecraft named Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 on an odyssey to the outer planets. Their primary mission, a close inspection of Jupiter and Saturn, was expected to last about five years. A rare alignment of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune allowed a probe to swing from one planet to the next by harnessing each planet's gravity. Exploiting it, the twins transmitted the first detailed images of distant moons, rings, and storms. [1] Voyager 2 remains the only spacecraft ever to have visited Uranus and Neptune.
Astonishingly, both probes remain operational nearly half a century later. In 2012, Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to cross into interstellar space, the region beyond the vast bubble of charged particles blown outward by the Sun; Voyager 2 followed in 2018. [2] Their signals, traveling at the speed of light, now take close to a day to reach Earth, and they arrive so feeble that only colossal dish antennas can detect them.
Sustaining such antiquated machines has become an exercise in ingenuity. The probes draw their electricity from the heat of decaying plutonium. [3] To conserve it, engineers have deactivated heaters and scientific instruments one by one, deliberating carefully over which measurements justify the cost. In late 2023, Voyager 1 began transmitting garbled strings of data. After months of painstaking detective work, the team traced the problem to a single failed memory chip. In 2024 it relocated the affected software to other parts of the memory, restoring the stream of scientific data. [4] "We repaired it by radio across billions of kilometers on a computer designed in the early 1970s," one engineer remarked.
Each Voyager also carries a gold-plated copper record containing sounds and images of Earth, intended for any sentient beings who might one day stumble upon it. The likelihood that anyone will is vanishingly small, but the record has proved illuminating in another way: it invites people on Earth to ponder what they would choose to convey about themselves to strangers. Sometime in the coming years the probes' power will finally ____, and they will fall silent and drift inexorably toward the stars.

Almost everyone has promised to finish a task by a certain date and then ruefully watched the deadline slip past. The psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky gave this ubiquitous experience a name in 1979: the planning fallacy. It is the tendency to underestimate how long a future task will take, even when we know that similar tasks have overrun in the past. The salient feature of the bias is not that we are sometimes wrong, but that our errors skew consistently in one direction.
Large public projects offer the most conspicuous examples. The Sydney Opera House was scheduled to open in 1963 at a modest cost but was completed a full decade late and at many times its original budget. Yet the bias is just as pervasive in private life. In one often-cited study, students asked to forecast when they would complete their theses took considerably longer than they had anticipated, and most missed even the date they had offered as a worst-case scenario.
Why do we persist in making the same mistake? When we plan, we are prone to envisage the particular steps of the task at hand, picturing <u>a smooth path</u> from start to finish. The interruptions, ailments, and setbacks that derailed earlier ventures seem like aberrations unlikely to recur, so we omit them from the forecast.
A widely endorsed remedy is to step outside the project and ask a different question: not how long this will take me but how long similar projects took others. Forecasters who begin from such ____ data and only then adjust for the idiosyncrasies of their own case tend to produce estimates that are less flattering but far more accurate.

For decades, the manufacture of sophisticated computer chips was left largely to the market, and the market clustered it in a handful of locales. By the early 2020s, most of the world's leading-edge chips were fabricated in Taiwan, while South Korea had become a dominant producer of memory chips. The acute shortages of 2021, which idled car factories from Germany to the United States, transformed this geography into a geopolitical preoccupation. Governments reasoned that chips were too vital to be left to chance.
What followed was a subsidy race. In 2022 the United States enacted the CHIPS and Science Act, which earmarked roughly $52 billion to bolster chip research and domestic manufacturing. The European Union adopted its own chips act the following year, and Japan offered lavish support to a new fabrication plant that Taiwan's TSMC built on the island of Kyushu. Resolved not to lag behind, South Korea expanded tax credits for its own producers.
Proponents contend that the money buys <u>insurance</u>. They observe that a single earthquake, blockade or conflict in East Asia could paralyze the supply of components on which nearly every modern industry depends. Dispersing production across several regions may inflate costs, but it makes the whole system more ____.
Skeptics remain unpersuaded. Chip foundries are extraordinarily costly, and their success depends on skilled engineers and intricate networks of suppliers that cannot be conjured up with grants alone. "When affluent governments bid against one another, companies may simply pocket subsidies from whichever country offers the most while taxpayers foot the bill," one trade economist cautioned. Some economists also fear that the race could culminate in a glut of factories producing more chips than the world can absorb.

Saw through the trunk of a venerable tree, and you will find a chronicle of its life inscribed in concentric rings. In temperate climates, a tree adds one ring annually: pale, rapidly grown wood in spring followed by darker, denser wood in late summer. Tallying the rings discloses the tree's age, but their genuine value resides in their width. [1] In arid regions, a year of abundant rainfall yields a wide ring, while a year of drought leaves only a slender line.
The science of reading these records is known as dendrochronology. It was pioneered in the early twentieth century by the American astronomer Andrew Ellicott Douglass. He was seeking evidence that cycles of solar activity influenced the Earth's climate, and he hoped that gnarled old trees in Arizona might have preserved a record of them. [2] His solar hypothesis never won wide acceptance, but his method proved enormously fruitful. Because all the trees in a region experience the same sequence of wet and dry years, they share a distinctive pattern of wide and narrow rings much like a bar code. By collating the overlapping patterns of living trees, old timbers, and preserved wood, researchers can extend a chronology far beyond the lifespan of any single tree.
In 1929, Douglass deployed such a chronology to date the wooden beams of ancient dwellings in the American Southwest, telling researchers in which years the buildings had been constructed. [3] Today the same technique is employed to date violins, panel paintings, and the timbers of medieval churches. Because the spruce top of a violin preserves the rings of the tree it came from, experts can judge whether an instrument ascribed to a renowned maker could plausibly have been built in his lifetime.
Tree rings have also become one of the most indispensable archives of past climate. Some bristlecone pines in the mountains of California are more than four thousand years old, and together with long-dead wood their rings record centuries of droughts that no instrument ever gauged. [4] Such records have shown that the American Southwest has endured droughts more protracted and more severe than any experienced in modern times. "That is a sobering lesson for planners who presume that the climate of the past century is a reliable guide to the future," one climatologist has said.

Few workplace experiments have garnered as much attention as the four-day week. In 2022 around sixty British companies ranging from software firms to a fish-and-chip shop consented to let their employees work four days a week for six months without any reduction in pay. The stipulation was that productivity should not decline.
The results were published the following year and were striking. Most participating companies reported that output held steady, staff reported diminished stress and fatigue, and fewer employees resigned. When the trial ended, the great majority of firms opted to retain the shorter week, at least for the time being. Trials in several other countries have yielded broadly comparable findings.
Skeptics counsel caution before drawing sweeping conclusions. "The companies volunteered to take part, so they were probably those most confident that the scheme would succeed," one labor economist noted. Many were small offices whose work could be readily reorganized. Hospitals, schools, and factories, where someone must be physically present, face far more formidable obstacles. And some of the gains may reflect the novelty of the experiment rather than an enduring transformation.
Still, the trials have reframed the debate. The question is no longer whether a shorter week is ____ at all, but for which kinds of work it makes sense and how it should be organized.

In a celebrated passage of his Confessions written around the year 400, Augustine describes watching Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, reading in silence: his eyes scanned the page while his voice and tongue remained still. Augustine evidently found the habit worth remarking upon, and for a long time historians took his surprise as conclusive proof that almost everyone in the ancient world read aloud.
The explanation seemed self-evident. Greek and Latin texts were commonly written as an unbroken chain of letters, with no gaps to mark where one word ended and the next began. Scholars argued that deciphering such a page required sounding it out, much as a child learning to read still does. Reading was therefore a communal and audible act, often performed for listeners rather than in private.
More recent scholarship has <u>complicated this tidy picture</u>. Sporadic references in ancient plays and letters suggest that silent reading, though perhaps less common, was by no means unknown. What astonished Augustine may have been not the silence itself but the bishop's refusal to share what he was reading with the visitors waiting before him.
Even so, there is scant doubt that the habit became far more prevalent in the Middle Ages. Scribes in Ireland and Britain who were transcribing a Latin they had not grown up speaking began to demarcate words with spaces, and the practice then gradually diffused across Europe. A page divided into words could be absorbed by the eye alone, quickly and ____. Silent reading in turn made the book a more personal companion that could harbor unorthodox ideas, intimate confessions or simply the reader's own unhurried thoughts.

Economists have long acknowledged that a dismal harvest can inflate the price of bread. What is novel is how frequently bad harvests now materialize, and how many crops they afflict at once. Pundits have coined an ungainly word for the result: <u>climateflation</u>, the upward pressure on prices engendered by a warmer and more erratic climate.
Recent years have furnished ample examples. Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana jointly cultivate more than half of the world's cocoa and suffered meager harvests after anomalous heat and torrential rains fostered disease, so in 2024 cocoa prices soared to record highs. This ratcheted up the cost of chocolate worldwide. In Spain, the foremost producer of olive oil, two consecutive years of drought slashed output, and supermarket prices for the oil more than doubled. Coffee, oranges, and rice have all endured similar upheavals.
For central banks, such price surges pose a vexing ____. "Raising interest rates can dampen demand but cannot make rain fall on parched fields or resurrect a ruined harvest," one central banker conceded. If food prices spike because of capricious weather, more stringent monetary policy may slow the economy without addressing the cause. Yet if central bankers disregard the shocks and they become chronic, households may come to anticipate permanently elevated inflation.
The burden is distributed inequitably. Affluent households devote only a modest share of their income to food, so a costlier chocolate bar is a trifling irritation. For impoverished families, particularly in countries that import most of their food, the same shocks can entail skipped meals. Adaptation, from drought-tolerant cultivars to more diversified sources of supply, will alleviate the strain. Yet few economists expect the pressure to dissipate while the climate continues to warm.

Why do zebras have stripes? The question has perplexed naturalists since the nineteenth century, and the conjectures offered have been almost as diverse as the animals' markings. Some speculated that the stripes camouflage zebras in tall grass or bewilder lions during a pursuit. Others thought they help the animals dissipate heat or enable them to recognize one another.
Over the past two decades, field observations and controlled experiments have tilted the debate toward a more prosaic explanation: flies. Biting flies such as horseflies transmit diseases that can be lethal to horses and their kin, and zebras inhabit regions where such insects proliferate.
In one trial in Britain, researchers draped horses in black-and-white striped coats. Flies approached the striped coats about as often as plain ones, but they rarely succeeded in alighting on them, apparently because the pattern disoriented them during the final moments of approach.
The other theories have not been entirely discarded, and stripes may fulfill more than one function. "Lions seem to have little difficulty catching zebras," one field biologist noted, a fact that undermines the notion of stripes as protection against formidable predators. The pattern that spawned so much speculation may owe its existence chiefly to some of the most diminutive creatures on the savanna.

"Watch the water, not the boat," my aunt said on the first morning, and for the rest of that summer she said very little else. She had sailed the lake behind her house for thirty years. When my parents dispatched me to stay with her at fifteen, sullen and convinced I would be bored, she simply handed me a life jacket and pointed at a small wooden dinghy moored at the dock.
I learned slowly and clumsily. I capsized twice in the first week, snarled the ropes so thoroughly that it took an hour to disentangle them, and once drifted so far downwind that she had to row out and tow me home. She never reproached me, but she never praised me either. When I finally managed a clean turn, she glanced up from her newspaper, nodded once and returned to her reading. I concluded she found me tedious.
In late August, we were halfway across the lake together when the wind veered without warning. The sky to the west assumed the color of a bruise, and gusts began to darken the water in patches that hurtled toward us. I reached for the tiller to surrender it to her, but she folded her arms and told me it was my boat. For twenty minutes I wrestled with the gusts, easing the sail out whenever a dark patch struck and steering us inch by inch toward the dock. My hands were raw and my heart was hammering when we bumped against the wood. "You watched the water," she said after she had secured the boat and stepped ashore.
It took me years to comprehend that afternoon. I had mistaken her silence for indifference, when it was something closer to <u>a vote of confidence</u>: she had been scrutinizing me all summer, and she had decided I was ready long before I believed it myself. I have taught many people to sail since then, and I still find it harder to stay silent than to dispense instructions. But I have learned that the most ____ thing a teacher can sometimes do is step back and let the student hold the tiller.

For most of history, blue was the most precious color a painter could employ. The finest blue pigment, ultramarine, was ground from lapis lazuli, a semi-precious stone quarried in the remote mountains of what is now northeastern Afghanistan. Its name, meaning 'beyond the sea,' evokes the arduous journey the stone made to reach European workshops. Extracting the pure pigment was laborious: the stone had to be pulverized, blended into a paste, and kneaded repeatedly to isolate the blue particles from impurities. At times, the result was more costly than gold.
Such extravagance shaped the symbolism of the color. In Renaissance Italy, patrons who commissioned altarpieces sometimes stipulated in their contracts how much ultramarine was to be used and on which figures, and the resplendent blue was customarily reserved for the robes of the Virgin Mary. A viewer did not need to peruse a contract to decipher the message: the most ____ material was devoted to the most sacred subject.
The color's exclusivity dissolved in the nineteenth century. In 1824 a French society offered a prize to anyone who could synthesize ultramarine at a reasonable price, and within a few years a chemist claimed it with a synthetic version. The new pigment was chemically virtually identical to the natural one and cost a small fraction as much.
Inexpensive blue revolutionized painting. Artists could now lavish it on skies and seas, and some later painters would construct entire works around it. Yet something was forfeited as well as gained. "Once any painter could afford it, ultramarine ceased to connote wealth or piety," one art historian has written. Blue became merely one color among many, cherished for its beauty rather than its price.

따로 증거를 요구했으니 '믿지 않는(incredulous)' 반응이에요. aquatic(물에 사는)·vegetarian(채식의)·mountainous(산이 많은)는 문맥과 관계없어요.

다음 빈칸에 들어갈 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.

금리가 올라 대출과 소비가 줄었으니 경제가 '휘청거리기(falter)' 시작했다는 말이에요. gargle(입을 헹구다)·knit(뜨개질하다)·solder(땜질하다)는 문맥과 관계없어요.

다음 빈칸에 들어갈 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.

12쪽짜리 서류를 다 쓰기 전에 포기했다니 절차가 '번거로운(cumbersome)' 것이에요. nocturnal(야행성의)·carnivorous(육식의)·maritime(바다의)은 문맥과 관계없어요.

다음 빈칸에 들어갈 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.

과학자를 나이 든 남성으로만 그리는 교과서가 고정관념을 '이어 가게 한다(perpetuate)'는 비판이에요. perforate(구멍을 내다)는 철자만 비슷하고, hibernate(겨울잠 자다)·cauterize(지져서 소독하다)는 문맥과 관계없어요.

다음 빈칸에 들어갈 가장 알맞은 것을 고르시오.

독자의 주의를 흩뜨려 지우는 세부이니 '관계없는, 군더더기(extraneous)'예요. amphibious(물과 뭍 양쪽의)·lunar(달의)·edible(먹을 수 있는)은 문맥과 관계없어요.

book : chapter ::
장(chapter)은 책의 한 부분이에요(전체 : 부분). 교향곡과 악장(movement)이 같아요. 작곡가와 교향곡은 '만든 사람 : 작품', 지휘자와 관현악단은 '이끄는 사람 : 이끄는 무리', violin : instrument 는 '종류 : 상위 개념'이에요.

주어진 단어 쌍과 관계가 가장 비슷한 것을 고르시오.
clay : potter ::
도공은 점토로 물건을 만들어요(재료 : 만드는 사람). 나무와 목수가 같아요. 끌과 조각가는 '도구 : 쓰는 사람', 작업장과 대장장이는 '일하는 곳 : 사람', 견습생과 장인은 '배우는 사람 : 가르치는 사람'이에요.

anatomist : body ::
해부학자는 몸을 연구해요(학자 : 연구 대상). 생태학자와 생태계가 같아요. 생물학자와 현미경은 '사람 : 도구', 언어학자와 통역사는 비슷한 분야의 다른 직업, 동물학자와 동물원은 '사람 : 일하는 곳'이에요.

asked 의 목적어인 간접의문문은 '접속사 whether + 주어 + 동사' 순서예요. 의문문처럼 would 를 앞으로 빼지 않아요.

다음 빈칸에 들어갈 가장 알맞은 표현을 고르시오.
____ in the remote village owns a smartphone, yet reliable internet access is still remarkably scarce.
almost 는 부사라 everyone 을 바로 꾸며요. every 뒤에는 단수 명사가 와야 해서 every people 은 틀려요.

다음 빈칸에 들어갈 가장 알맞은 표현을 고르시오.
The ambiguous new policy has caused ____ confusion among small-business proprietors than officials had expected.
confusion 은 셀 수 없는 명사라 much 로 비교급 more 를 강조해요. many more 는 셀 수 있는 복수 명사 앞에 써요.

다음 빈칸에 들어갈 가장 알맞은 표현을 고르시오.
____ the invention of the printing press that made the rapid dissemination of unorthodox ideas possible.
'바로 ~였다'를 강조하는 It was ~ that 구문이에요. 강조할 말이 It was 와 that 사이에 들어가요.

다음 빈칸에 들어갈 가장 알맞은 표현을 고르시오.
The new model is ____ the previous one, but it is far more economical on long journeys.
원급 비교는 as + 원급 + as 이고, '거의'를 뜻하는 nearly 는 그 덩어리 맨 앞에 와요(nearly as powerful as).

다음 빈칸에 들어갈 가장 알맞은 표현을 고르시오.
Torrential rains over the weekend caused the river ____ its banks in several places.
cause 는 'cause + 목적어 + to부정사' 꼴로 써요. 원형은 make·let 같은 사역동사 뒤에 와요.

다음 빈칸에 들어갈 가장 알맞은 표현을 고르시오.
The researchers found the results ____ and decided to replicate the experiment with a larger sample.
결과가 사람을 '혼란스럽게 하는' 것이라 현재분사 confusing 이에요. 분사를 꾸미는 말은 부사 deeply 예요.

다음 빈칸에 들어갈 가장 알맞은 표현을 고르시오.
This is the tranquil coastal town ____ the composer spent the final years of his life in seclusion.
빈칸 뒤가 빠진 것 없는 완전한 절이라 장소를 나타내는 '전치사 + 관계대명사' in which(= where)가 맞아요. 전치사 뒤에는 that 을 못 써요.

다음 빈칸에 들어갈 가장 알맞은 표현을 고르시오.
My older sister has never ventured outside the country, and ____.
부정문에 '나도 그렇다'고 이을 때는 neither + 조동사 + 주어 순서예요. 앞이 현재완료라 have 를 써요.

다음 빈칸에 들어갈 가장 알맞은 표현을 고르시오.
____ the warning earlier, the villagers could have escaped before the devastating flood arrived.
주절이 could have escaped(가정법 과거완료)라 조건절은 If they had received 예요. if 를 빼면 Had they received 로 도치해요. They had received 는 접속사 없이 절 두 개를 콤마로만 잇게 돼요.

다음 빈칸에 들어갈 가장 알맞은 표현을 고르시오.
Looking back on his illustrious career, he wishes he ____ more time with his children when they were young.
지나간 일(when they were young)을 아쉬워하는 wish 뒤에는 과거완료 had spent 가 와요.

다음 빈칸에 들어갈 가장 알맞은 표현을 고르시오.
Because the instructions were so lucid, ____ needed any help assembling the shelves.
any 가 있으니 부정의 뜻이 필요해 few(거의 없는)가 맞아요. 셀 수 있는 customers 라 little 은 쓸 수 없어요.

다음 빈칸에 들어갈 가장 알맞은 표현을 고르시오.
Scholarships will be awarded to ____ financial need and exemplary academic records.
'~하는 사람들'은 those who 로 쓰고 바로 뒤에 관계절 동사 demonstrate 가 와요. 전치사 to 의 목적어가 those 예요.

다음 빈칸에 들어갈 가장 알맞은 표현을 고르시오.
There is ____ habitual exercise slows the deterioration of memory in old age.
evidence 의 내용을 설명하는 완전한 절이 이어지니 동격 that 이 맞아요. which 는 뒤에 빠진 성분이 있어야 해요.

다음 빈칸에 들어갈 가장 알맞은 표현을 고르시오.
Many veteran employees are not yet used ____ online tools for every meeting.
be used to(~에 익숙하다)의 to 는 전치사라 바로 뒤에 동명사 relying 이 오고, rely 에 붙는 on 이 이어져요.

다음 밑줄 친 부분 중 어법상 틀린 것을 고르시오.
The museum, ①<u>which</u> reopened after a protracted renovation, now exhibits several paintings ②<u>that</u> ③<u>was</u> ④<u>long</u> hidden in storage vaults beneath the main gallery.
that 의 선행사는 복수 several paintings 라 관계절 동사도 were 가 돼야 해요.

다음 밑줄 친 부분 중 어법상 틀린 것을 고르시오.
The delegates ①<u>postponed</u> the meeting ②<u>until</u> the following morning, ③<u>exhausting</u> by the arduous journey and ④<u>eager</u> to reach a definitive agreement after a night's rest.
대표단은 긴 여정에 '지친' 것이라 과거분사 exhausted 로 써야 해요. by 가 수동의 단서예요.

다음 밑줄 친 부분 중 어법상 틀린 것을 고르시오.
The report cautioned that the region's water supply ①<u>is</u> ②<u>increasingly</u> ③<u>vulnerable</u> to drought and called for ④<u>urgently</u> investment in reservoirs and pipelines.
명사 investment 를 꾸미는 자리라 부사 urgently 가 아니라 형용사 urgent 가 와야 해요.

다음 밑줄 친 부분 중 어법상 틀린 것을 고르시오.
Scientists ①<u>have identified</u> a hitherto unknown species of frog ②<u>which</u> vivid blue skin may help ③<u>warn</u> predators ④<u>that</u> it is poisonous.
개구리'의' 파란 피부라는 소유 관계라 which 가 아니라 whose 가 맞아요(whose vivid blue skin).

다음 밑줄 친 부분 중 어법상 틀린 것을 고르시오.
The charity, ①<u>which</u> was ②<u>find</u> by a group of retired teachers in 1998, ③<u>now</u> provides free tutoring to ④<u>more than</u> two thousand underprivileged children.
'설립되다'는 found(세우다)의 수동 was founded 예요. find(찾다)와 헷갈리기 쉬워요.

다음 밑줄 친 부분 중 어법상 틀린 것을 고르시오.
The ancient manuscript, ①<u>which</u> scholars ②<u>had believed</u> lost for centuries, ③<u>was</u> recently found in a secluded monastery library and is currently ④<u>restoring</u> by conservators in Rome.
원고는 전문가들에 의해 '복원되는' 것이라 is currently being restored 처럼 수동 진행형이 돼야 해요.

다음 밑줄 친 부분 중 어법상 틀린 것을 고르시오.
①<u>Much</u> residents of the historic quarter ②<u>complained</u> that the stringent new parking rules ③<u>were</u> introduced without ④<u>adequate</u> consultation with the people most affected by them.
residents 는 셀 수 있는 복수 명사라 Much 가 아니라 Many 가 와야 해요.

다음 밑줄 친 부분 중 어법상 틀린 것을 고르시오.
The committee will ①<u>discuss</u> the proposal next week, but several members have ②<u>already expressed</u> reservations and plan to ③<u>oppose to</u> it ④<u>unless</u> the exorbitant costs are reduced.
oppose 는 목적어를 바로 받는 타동사라 to 를 쓰지 않아요(oppose it). be opposed to 와 헷갈리기 쉬워요.

다음 밑줄 친 부분 중 어법상 틀린 것을 고르시오.
Although the old phones were bulkier, many users ①<u>insist</u> that they ②<u>were</u> ③<u>more durable</u> than the sleek new ④<u>one</u> sold in stores today.
받는 말이 복수 phones 라 대명사도 복수 ones 로 써야 해요.

다음 밑줄 친 부분 중 어법상 틀린 것을 고르시오.
The ferocious storm, which ①<u>is expected</u> to weaken ②<u>as</u> it moves northward over cooler waters, ③<u>knocking</u> out power to thousands of households ④<u>last night</u>.
주어 The ferocious storm 의 동사가 없어요. which 절은 콤마 안에서 끝나니 knocking 을 정동사 knocked 로 고쳐야 문장이 완성돼요.

다음 밑줄 친 부분 중 어법상 틀린 것을 고르시오.
Only after the floodwaters ①<u>had receded</u> ②<u>did</u> officials ③<u>realized</u> how many homes in the inundated valley ④<u>had been</u> destroyed.
Only after ~ 가 앞에 와서 did 가 주어 앞으로 나온 도치문이에요. did 뒤에는 동사원형 realize 가 와요.

다음 밑줄 친 부분 중 어법상 틀린 것을 고르시오.
Many companies now ①<u>allow</u> employees ②<u>working</u> from home two days a week, a policy ③<u>that</u> was unusual ④<u>before</u> the pandemic.
allow 는 'allow + 목적어 + to부정사' 꼴이라 to work 가 맞아요.

다음 밑줄 친 부분 중 어법상 틀린 것을 고르시오.
Scientists ①<u>were</u> astonished to discover ②<u>that</u> the bacteria ③<u>could</u> survive in extreme conditions ④<u>what</u> would kill most other organisms.
선행사 conditions 가 있으니 what 이 아니라 관계대명사 that(또는 which)이 와야 해요.

다음 밑줄 친 부분 중 어법상 틀린 것을 고르시오.
Arguing that low-paid workers ①<u>needed</u> help ②<u>coping</u> with soaring prices for food and rent, the government ③<u>finally</u> ④<u>rose</u> the minimum wage last year.
최저임금을 '올리다'는 목적어를 받는 타동사 raise 의 과거 raised 예요. rise 는 자동사예요.

다음 밑줄 친 부분 중 어법상 틀린 것을 고르시오.
Every summer, ①<u>thousands of</u> tourists ②<u>visit</u> the picturesque island, and ③<u>hundred of</u> local families ④<u>depend on</u> the revenue they bring.
막연히 '수백의'라고 할 때는 hundreds of 로 복수형을 써요.
